```{r}
#| label: setup

library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    fig.asp = 0.618,
    fig.align = "center",
    out.width = "100%",
    fig.retina = 3,
    fig.path = "./images/01-intro/",
    message = FALSE,
    warning = FALSE,
    global.par = TRUE
)
options(
  htmltools.dir.version = FALSE,
  dplyr.print_min = 6, 
  dplyr.print_max = 6,
  tibble.width = 80,
  width = 80,
  digits = 4
  )
hook_output <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("output")
knitr::knit_hooks$set(output = function(x, options) {
  lines <- options$output.lines
  if (is.null(lines)) {
    return(hook_output(x, options))  # pass to default hook
  }
  x <- unlist(strsplit(x, "\n"))
  more <- "..."
  if (length(lines)==1) {        # first n lines
    if (length(x) > lines) {
      # truncate the output, but add ....
      x <- c(head(x, lines), more)
    }
  } else {
    x <- c(more, x[lines], more)
  }
  # paste these lines together
  x <- paste(c(x, ""), collapse = "\n")
  hook_output(x, options)
})
ggplot2::theme_set(ggplot2::theme_bw(base_size = 16))
```

# Introduction to Statistical Computing

<h2> What is computational statistics? </h2>
<h2> The R environment and reproducible workflow </h2>
<h2> R objects: vectors, matrices, arrays, lists, data frames </h2>
<h2> Functions, control flow, and vectorization </h2>
<h2> Graphics and importing data </h2>

::: notes
- Rizzo, Chapter 1. The goal today is to get everybody on the same page with R so that the rest of the semester we can focus on statistical ideas.
- Each slide that has code is live R code; open the .qmd and run it chunk by chunk.
:::

## Computational Statistics vs. Statistical Computing

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Statistical computing**

- Numerical methods *inside* statistical software
- Floating-point arithmetic, linear algebra, optimization, root finding, numerical integration
- How `lm()`, `optim()`, `integrate()` actually work
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Computational statistics**

- Statistical methods that are *made possible* by computing
- Simulation, Monte Carlo, bootstrap, jackknife, permutation tests, MCMC, density estimation, clustering, EM
- Replace hard math with many cheap computations
:::
::::

::: question
Why can't we just derive a formula? What happens when the sampling distribution of $\hat\theta$ is unknown, the sample is small, or the model has no closed-form likelihood?
:::

## Why R?

- Free, open source, runs everywhere (Windows, macOS, Linux)
- Designed by statisticians for data analysis: vectors, data frames, formulas, models
- 20,000+ packages on CRAN (and Bioconductor, GitHub)
- Excellent graphics: base, `lattice`, `ggplot2`
- Reproducible documents: R Markdown / **Quarto** (these slides!)
- Interfaces to C/C++ (`Rcpp`), Python (`reticulate`), databases, the web

::: alert
In this course: **R first**, with Python supplements when they illuminate a point. Everything you see on a slide is code you can run.
:::

## The Working Environment

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **IDE:** RStudio or Positron
- **Projects:** one folder per assignment (`.Rproj`)
- **Quarto documents** (`.qmd`) mix text, math, and code
- **Packages:** `install.packages("boot")` once; `library(boot)` every session
- **Help:** `?mean`, `help.search("bootstrap")`, `example(sample)`, vignettes
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: instructions
**Reproducibility checklist**

- Never rely on objects in your global environment
- Set a seed: `set.seed(4750)`
- Keep data files in the project folder; use relative paths
- Render the whole document before you submit
- Report `sessionInfo()` when asking for help
:::
:::
::::

## R as a Calculator

```{r}
2 + 3 * 4
exp(1); log(100, base = 10); sqrt(2)^2 == 2
isTRUE(all.equal(sqrt(2)^2, 2))  # floating point! (Ch 13)
choose(10, 3); factorial(5); gamma(5)
x <- c(3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6)
mean(x); var(x); sd(x); median(x)
```

::: notes
- Note sqrt(2)^2 == 2 is FALSE. We come back to this in numerical methods (Ch 13). Use all.equal for floating point comparisons.
:::

## Vectors and Vectorized Operations

- Almost everything in R is a vector; operations are *element-wise* and recycle.

```{r}
x <- 1:10
x^2
sum(x[x %% 2 == 0])          # logical indexing
seq(0, 1, by = 0.25); rep(c("a", "b"), times = 3)
y <- c(height = 1.80, weight = 82)   # named vector
y["weight"]
```

. . .

::: tip
Vectorized code is shorter, clearer, and usually much faster than an explicit loop. We will benchmark this in Chapter 15.
:::

## Probability Functions: d, p, q, r

```{r}
#| echo: false
fun <- data.frame(
  Prefix = c("`d`", "`p`", "`q`", "`r`"),
  Meaning = c("density / pmf  $f(x)$", "cdf  $F(x)=P(X\\le x)$", "quantile  $F^{-1}(p)$", "random generation"),
  Example = c("`dnorm(0)`", "`pnorm(1.96)`", "`qnorm(0.975)`", "`rnorm(5)`")
)
knitr::kable(fun, escape = FALSE)
```

```{r}
dnorm(0); pnorm(1.96); qnorm(0.975)
set.seed(4750); rnorm(5, mean = 10, sd = 2)
dbinom(3, size = 10, prob = 0.4); ppois(2, lambda = 3); qexp(0.5, rate = 2)
```

Suffixes: `norm`, `binom`, `pois`, `exp`, `gamma`, `beta`, `t`, `chisq`, `f`, `unif`, `geom`, `nbinom`, `cauchy`, `weibull`, `lnorm`, ...

## Example 1.1: `sample()` and Simulated Dice

```{r}
set.seed(1)
rolls <- sample(1:6, size = 1000, replace = TRUE)
table(rolls) / 1000
```

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.35
barplot(table(rolls) / 1000, col = "#FFCC00", ylim = c(0, 0.25),
        main = "Relative frequency of 1000 fair die rolls")
abline(h = 1/6, lty = 2, col = "#003366", lwd = 2)
```

## Data Frames: Example 1.2 (`iris`)

```{r}
str(iris)
head(iris, 4)
summary(iris$Petal.Length)
```

## Working with Data Frames

```{r}
# subset rows and columns
iris[iris$Species == "virginica" & iris$Sepal.Length > 7.5, c("Sepal.Length", "Petal.Length")]
# group summaries
aggregate(Petal.Length ~ Species, data = iris, FUN = mean)
with(iris, tapply(Sepal.Width, Species, sd))
```

## Matrices and Arrays: Examples 1.3 - 1.4

```{r}
A <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)       # filled by column
A
dim(A); t(A)
B <- matrix(c(2, 1, 1, 3), 2, 2)
B %*% A                          # matrix product
solve(B)                         # inverse
x <- array(1:24, dim = c(2, 3, 4)); x[2, 3, 4]
```

## Example 1.5: `iris3` as a 3-d Array

```{r}
dim(iris3)                         # 50 flowers x 4 measurements x 3 species
apply(iris3, MARGIN = c(2, 3), FUN = mean)   # means by variable and species
```

::: question
How would you compute the same table from the `iris` data frame?
:::

. . .

```{r}
t(sapply(split(iris[, 1:4], iris$Species), colMeans))
```

## Lists: Examples 1.6 - 1.8

```{r}
set.seed(4750)
n <- 50; x <- sample(0:1, size = n, replace = TRUE)
r <- rle(x)                       # run length encoding (a list!)
str(r)
max(r$lengths)                    # longest run
w <- list(name = "Geometric", p = 0.2, values = rgeom(5, 0.2))
w$values; w[["p"]]; names(w)
```

## Writing Functions

```{r}
sumdice <- function(n, sides = 6) {
  # simulate the sum of two dice n times
  k <- sample(1:sides, size = n, replace = TRUE) +
       sample(1:sides, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  return(k)
}
set.seed(2027)
s <- sumdice(10000)
round(table(s) / length(s), 3)
```

::: question
What is the exact pmf of the sum of two fair dice? Compare with the simulated frequencies.
:::

## Control Flow and the `apply` Family

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
x <- c(-2, 0, 3)
for (xi in x) {
  if (xi < 0) {
    cat(xi, "is negative\n")
  } else if (xi == 0) {
    cat(xi, "is zero\n")
  } else cat(xi, "is positive\n")
}
ifelse(x > 0, "pos", "non-pos")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
m <- matrix(rnorm(20), 4, 5)
apply(m, 1, max)          # rows
sapply(1:5, function(k) k^2)
vapply(iris[, 1:4], median, numeric(1))
Map(function(a, b) a + b, 1:3, 4:6) |> unlist()
```
:::
::::

## A First Simulation: Law of Large Numbers

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.4
set.seed(4750)
n <- 5000
x <- rexp(n, rate = 2)           # E(X) = 1/2
running_mean <- cumsum(x) / seq_len(n)
plot(running_mean, type = "l", log = "x", lwd = 2, col = "#003366",
     xlab = "n", ylab = "running mean", main = "LLN: sample mean of Exp(2)")
abline(h = 0.5, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
```

# Graphics

## Example 1.9: Parallel Boxplots (base R)

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.45
boxplot(len ~ dose, data = ToothGrowth, col = c("#FFCC00", "#88A0C8", "#F26BAA"),
        xlab = "Vitamin C dose (mg/day)", ylab = "Tooth length",
        main = "ToothGrowth: tooth length by dose")
```

## Examples 1.10 - 1.12: Scatterplots, Colors, Symbols

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.45
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Petal.Width, pch = as.integer(iris$Species),
     col = as.integer(iris$Species) + 1, xlab = "Petal length", ylab = "Petal width")
legend("topleft", legend = levels(iris$Species), pch = 1:3, col = 2:4, bty = "n")
pairs(iris[, 1:4], col = as.integer(iris$Species) + 1, pch = 20, cex = 0.6)
```

## Example 1.13: `ggplot2` Boxplots and Violin Plots

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.4
library(patchwork)
p1 <- ggplot(ToothGrowth, aes(factor(dose), len, fill = supp)) + geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "dose", y = "length")
p2 <- ggplot(ToothGrowth, aes(factor(dose), len)) + geom_violin(fill = "#FFCC00") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5) + labs(x = "dose", y = "length")
p1 + p2
```

## Example 1.14: MPG by Engine Displacement

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.45
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "loess", se = TRUE, color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Engine displacement (L)", y = "Highway MPG")
```

## Examples 1.15 - 1.17: Importing and Exporting Data

```{r}
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(iris[1:5, ], tmp, row.names = FALSE)   # export
dat <- read.csv(tmp)                               # import
str(dat)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
# other common readers
read.table("data/file.txt", header = TRUE)        # whitespace-delimited
readr::read_csv("data/file.csv")                  # tidyverse reader
readxl::read_excel("data/file.xlsx")
read.table("https://www.example.edu/data.dat")    # straight from the web
```

::: tip
Always inspect after importing: `str()`, `head()`, `summary()`, and check for `NA`.
:::

## Python Supplement: the Same Ideas in `numpy`

```{.python}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(4750)
x = rng.exponential(scale=0.5, size=5000)     # Exp(rate = 2)
running_mean = np.cumsum(x) / np.arange(1, x.size + 1)
print(running_mean[[9, 99, 999, 4999]])
```

- In Quarto, Python chunks run through `reticulate` (conda env `py39` in my setup).
- Note: R and Python random-number streams differ even with the same seed.

## Summary

::: instructions
- R is a vectorized language: think in vectors, matrices, and lists.
- `d/p/q/r` functions give you every standard distribution.
- Functions + `sample()` + loops/`apply` are enough to simulate almost anything.
- Graphics: base R for quick looks, `ggplot2` for layered, publication-quality plots.
- Reproducibility: projects, relative paths, seeds, Quarto.
:::
